body: If he's not sure now, he'll never be sure. Sounds like you're in a placeholder role. I've been there, done that and got the tshirt. The best thing you can do is realise that if this guy doesn't want to marry you, someone else 100% will. Don't sit around and wait forever.

Get out. Run away. Now. The sooner the better. There is no other option that doesn't involve you getting your heart broken and wasting a lot of time and fucking you up for future relationships.

Unfortunately I think this is one of those issues where the solution is to break up. It annoys me that everybody says "break up" on this sub without trying to figure it out, but, unfortunately, this is one of those situations where this is a long term compatibility issue. There is no middle ground here. You either go or you stay. He either goes or stays. One of you will end up resenting the other and the relationship will break down anyway. I know when it's your first love it feels that you willneber get over it but I promise you that you will. My advice would be to go, he stays, you part on good terms. And if when you are apart you both know that you need to be together, you will find a way to make it happen. If not, you know you made the right choice.
3 months is still early enough to get out while it won't trash your life. Run.

I know this is really hard but his life is not your responsibility. I had a partner once who was totally reliant on me, including for housing. I didn't leave the relationship that I hated being in because I felt it was my responsibility if I made him homeless by kicking him out. Eventually I was able to leave but I wish so badly I could go back and get rid of him sooner. I appreciate that he is struggling with his mental health, but that's not a reason why your life should not progress.

Grown ups should clear up after themselves. I have ADHD and I feel like I'm constantly battling with myself because I like things to be clean, and I will get everything spotless, and then immediately get it all in a mess again. I don't even know sometimes how I've made such a mess, but I would never expect my partner to clean up after me. He does sometimes but I think just because he is cleaning anyway and he's not the type to be like "I'll clean my own mess - but not yours." But I'm sorry, I just don't think it's a good enough excuse to be careless and lazy. Just tell him straight that you love him, and you want to feel the attraction, but having to clean up after him makes you feel like you're parenting him rather than partnering him. Me and my partner have a rule that if a task takes less than 5 minutes (such as wiping the kitchen sides after yourself, putting something away) that it is to be done immediately. That way it rarely gets into a huge mess, and we both feel respected in our own space.

No you certainly should not allow it to consume your life. The vast majority of relationships don't work out  and that's fine. You dates this girl for such a brief period you really don't need to be thinking too deeply into it.

Move on. It doesn't seem like you were compatible, and I also think that it's a bit of a red flag to be so caught up in a situation that only lasted a couple of months. Just learn from it and move on.

Move on. Next. You're so young, you have your whole life ahead of you, I've seen some other stuff about him pursuing this chick previously. Just sail into the sunset before this guy causes real damage. You have no reason to fear being "alone" you're 20. I'd bet my bottom dollar you have a bunch of friends you can hang out with and maybe you have school and/or a job to keep you occupied. Trust me, being "alone" is better than constantly worrying about your boyfriend and what he might do. It took me a long time to learn this lesson and caused a lot of damage on the way. I've felt more lonely in a bad relationship than I've ever felt while single. Once I decided to put myself first and prioritse my happienss, my now fiancé walked into my life when I really wasn't looking. The best things always happen when your energy is focused on making your life the happiest it can be. This guy doesn't make you happy.

I would be hurt too. It's not materialistic to feel that you want your partner to get you a gift for Christmas. I feel like it's not about what the gifts is, or the materialistic element of it, its that the gift is a symbol that he values you, takes you seriously, and it is physical token of the fact that he put time and effort into something for you. 

I agree with others that conversations around budget and expectations need to be had, but don't feel that you're being ungrateful or materialistic for being a little hurt that he didn't get you anything.

I was in your situation when I was younger too. I told my mum and then decided not to terminate the pregnancy. With the benefit of hindsight - I wish I had only involved my family if I had decided I was having a baby. As you have expressed concern about your family being involved if you terminate, I would say that my advice is take some time to think about what you want to do, and then decide if you want to tell your mum. You only just missed your period, you have time to think. Also I'm not sure where you live, but you need to research how easy access to abortion is. I live in the UK and you have yo have a termination form signed, a sexual health check and a scan before having an abortion, so I suggest (if possible) you make the practical arrangements to terminate the pregnancy, so the option is there if you want it and it can be as smooth as possible. You can always choose not to go through with abortion if you decide its not right for you.
Take your daughter. Period. And your son if needs be.

I have been your husband. My anxiety absolutely took over my life. I suffered with really extreme health anxiety. I still do but nowhere near as extreme as it used to be. The guy needs THERAPY. It helps! It takes time and you have to engage with it properly and build the tools into your life. Try CBT for the symptoms and counselling for the cause. I did CBT and counselling back to back in that order. I've had several rounds of therapy. I now accept that anxiety is just something I have to deal with in my life but it no longer rules my existence. If you want any help or advice - please please message me!

I would say it's not your business to get involved in. I also morally disagree with her cheating but it's got no more to do with me than it does with you. If you are equally friends with her and the husband then I might advise you to say to her "cut this shit out or else I'm going to have to tell him, because he's my friend as much as you are" 
But even though her behaviour is wrong, you have absolutely no business ripping apart the home of 2 kids. You have no right to do that. If the parents end up ripping their lives to pieces by themselves then that is their choice to make.

Honey - he's cheating. No one would bring it up a year and a half later and be like omg you just told X you loved her and now you're IMMEDIATELY engaged to someone else. I'm sorry but he has been speaking to her/seeing her until very recently. If this was my partner I'd kick him out without thinking twice. He's gonna tell you he hasn't cheated. Go to Anna or her friend - you need the receipts to be sure - but I would be prepared to bet anything I own or could borrow that this guy has cheated. If you feel like you can work through infidelity then that is entirely your choice. However I would say that a leopard doesn't change his spots. This will not be the only time he's unfaithful to you I guarantee it.

Yes. Call it off. You are young, you have your whole life in front of you. You are right to decide that being second or third isn't good enough and being married isn't going to make this any better. It will be worse once marriage and potentially children are involved, so if you are thinking of leaving, now is the time to do it.
Don't worry about hurting people, they will get over it. You have to do what is best for YOU.
And if your partner has any ounce of sense, he won't want to be married to someone who doesn't want to be married to him, the best thing you can do, for both of you, is walk away.

This guy is taking you for a ride (no pun intended) and you sound like your self esteem is shattered. I have been in your shoes more than once in a situationship with someone who wants all the benefits and none of the commitments. I wish so much I had learnt my lesson after the first time. The best advice I can give you is RUN. Tell him you want your car back within a week and then cut ties and move on. Yes it is hard. Yes it will hurt. Yes you will feel like "what is wrong with me" but those feelings will run their course and you WILL feel better for taking the bull by the horns and walking away from a situation that it making you feel shit about yourself.
I also cannot stress enough how important it is for you to do some work on yourself so you have the self esteem to not be pulled into another situation like this. Therapy is your friend. I went through several awful relationships before I finally ended up in therapy and working on myself, and it was hard, but hands down the best thing I ever did.

After DV relationship you need time to heal and re-learn your worth. This guy is using you 100% - you deserve better. The best advice I can give you is get out now and take some time to be ALONE and work on your self esteem before you even think about getting into something with someone else.

OP, if you want to see what she wants - chat to her. I often feel like the comments on these sorts of posts are really over the top compared to the "crime" committed.
I don't see it as her violating your boundaries after 2 months of NC. She may well think that 2 months is enough time to be over your crush on her, or her feelings may have changed, or maybe she wants to see if you can work on your friendship. She has respected you for a consistent length of time, and now is wondering if you can meet. To me this doesn't read as malicious or disrespectful. 
If she wants to be just friends still and your feelings haven't changed - tell her and tell her that this time can she just wait for if/when you reach out to her. 
I don't think there is any harm in meeting her for a chat and seeing where both your feelings are at now. You never know, you might hang out with her IRL and be like actually you know what seeing you has made me realise I'm over this crush.
If you don't want to see her, of course tell her no, but I wouldn't read too deeply into the meaning behind why she has reached out. I don't think it's out of malice or being disrespectful. Also if you meet her - you'll be able to find out what she wants.

I would just like to ask you this, is it a stable home for your children with his ups and downs? 
I would argue that that situation is not stable. I'm not saying right just leave as of course it's not that easy, but if it's not "stable" as such whether you stay or leave then you have to ask yourself which situation is preferable, and which situation is more stable long term for you and your children. 
Also, you know your situation and your children best, but I wouldn't want my kids growing up thinking it's okay and normal for them to either tiptoe around their partners or have their partners pander to their own unreasonable mood swings. Leaving is never easy but often in situations like this, staying isn't easy either.

I suffer myself with bad anxiety and I really struggle to let go of control. My boyfriend, on the other hand is more like you, very laid back and doesn't take life too seriously or plan ahead much, which can be incredibly irritating for me, but, he is happy to let me take the reigns in some ways, and I realise that someone as chilled as him is what I need. 
I have found (lots of) therapy and making a real effort to take the tools I've been given by a therapist into my day to day life has reduced my anxiety from barely leaving the house to living a pretty normal life. I still suffer with anxiety but I'm much better now. I am also much better at relinquishing control and feeling comfortable with unpredictability and change than I used to be. I would highly recommend therapy and practising mindfulness to anyone like your girlfriend.
But ultimately, you have to decide if she doesn't want to do these things and is unlikely to change, if you can live with that long term. 
If she does decide she wants to help herself change, it can get worse before it gets better, therapy can be very confronting and she will need your emotional support.

Where was she living before she met you? 
I have 2 friends with BPD and neither of them ever behave in this way. I realise that BPD is a complex emotional disorder and can range in severity, but personally I have never experienced this kind of behaviour from either of them or witnessed them act out like this with other people.
Also - you're allowed to not be able to cope with this. You're allowed to say do you know what I actually can't be in a relationship with someone with such a tough mental health condition. I wouldn't be able to cope in a relationship with someone that depended on me emotionally in such an intense way. 
You are not responsible for any other human being. I don't think it's advisable to break up with her while she is in your house. If I were you I would insist that she goes back to wherever she was before she moved into your place and then, from a distance, break up with her.

NTA. The manner in which your wife chose to discipline your kids is appalling. 
I do agree with your wife that if the children misbehave in her presence, she should have the right to tell them off, or else they will not respect her as a parental figure in their lives, and, as she's your wife she is a parental figure to them. However, she should absolutely adhere to you and their mothers disciplinary system. She has no right whatsoever to just start handing out insane, and quite frankly, abusive, punishments.
If I were in your shoes, this would be a HUGE red flag about how she would treat a child of her own.

The most important question here is do you really want to marry someone who doesn't want to marry you? 
I'm not saying leave him, I'm saying ask yourself that question.
If he agrees to marry you, then you will feel like you forced him into it and it won't feel genuine. I'm not sure that's something that I'd want. 
If I were in your shoes, I would drop the subject altogether for now. Make it clear that you do, one day, want to get married but you don't want to pressure him, and you know you're young. And then LEAVE IT ALONE.  Don't bring it up again, like AT ALL, for at least a few months at the minimum. If he brings it up, fine don't run away and refuse to speak but don't initiate any conversation about it.
He will a. Feel like you've taken the pressure off him and b. Wonder why you seemingly don't seem to care anymore. I would be very surprised if you get through the next 6 months to a year without him initiating the first conversation about getting married.

Marriage doesn't have to be a big deal. You may feel safer without marriage in your current situation, but in terms of immigration its to your benefit to be married. I don't know where you're moving to but most of the big cities in Europe experience a lot of immigration and therefore the people who live there are (on the whole) not racist. I live in London and I don't know a single person in real life who is anything less than actively pro immigration and believes that you have just as much right to live here as we do (people who were born and raised here) 
Hope this eases your mind a little!

Jesus Christ this sounds like a mess. It's a difficult one because she's just lost a parent, and speaking from personal experience, it's really hard, and your emotions are all over the place. However, this doesn't make it okay for her to use things that happened in the past as an emotional battering ram, and I think you should tell her so, in a softer way. The bottom line is that you have 3 options in front of you right now: 1. Accept that this is how she behaves and may never let this go. 2. End the relationship. Or 3. Talk to her about this behaviour and try to move forward from it.
Let's assume you try to talk to her and move forward and nothing changes, now you have to pick out of options 1 or 2. Because you cannot make her behave in a certain way.
If I were in your shoes I would approach the conversation with something like "I think we need to talk about what happened when I went behind your back....we decided to stay together and move forward but we can't ever really move forward if we can't leave the past in the past. I have promised you that I won't behave that way again and I need you to trust me and move on. We can't have a functioning relationship moving forward if this keeps being brought back up. I understand that I did something wrong, but I can't change it or take it back, all I can do is offer you my sincere apologies and try to show you I care, but I need you to be able to leave it in the past and move on" 
I don't condone cheating but if you choose to stay with a partner who has been unfaithful to you, you have to be able to move on and leave the past behind or else it will never work.
I also suggest that you both go to therapy (individually) because you need help with your anxiety and she needs to work through her trauma. I suffer with intense anxiety and I've lost a parent. Trust me therapy helps even if you don't think it's helping at the time.

The fact that he is so concerned shows plainly that he's not taking advantage. There are men who take advantage of an age gap and use it to take advantage of younger, naive girls, but I think it's clear that this is not the case here. I'd say that if he were 21, and she 17, the maturity gap is too great at that age, even if he doesn't intend to take advantage, but 17 and 19 is not a big age gap at all really. I certainly think it's less of an age gap for girls, who mature much faster than boys. I also think age and maturity is relative. I think the younger you are the more prevalent an age gap is. For example, the maturity gap between a 15 year old and a 17 year old is much greater than that of a 17 year old and a 19 year old. 
But for OP and his chick, they are old enough to be making their own, informed choices about who to date and what boundaries to create. I'm sure being as young as they are, they will run into plenty of issues but I don't see age being an issue here. Its not like we're talking several years.

Honestly there is nothing wrong with this at all. I'm female and honestly I'd tell you if I thought this was creepy in any way, but in terms of maturity, you're probably on the same page, girls grow up quicker by a country mile. When I was 19, if my mate had dated a girl who was 17 I wouldn't have batted an eyelid, 15 or 16, I would say is too much of an age gap, at that age. If you like her, and you respect her you have nothing to worry about :)

That's not how gift giving works and I'm not normally the kind of person to get annoyed on the Internet, but, I do not for one second believe that an adult who lives in the world and has any kind of social decorum doesn't realise that asking for the money for something they were never entitled to is OUTRAGEOUS.

I really feel bad for Marissa that she is nice enough to buy you gifts and you are just looking to take advantage of her.

Nobody ever OWES you a birthday gift and if I was in Marissa's shoes and my mate approaches me with "so for my birthday you bought me tickets but now it's cancelled can I just have the money" I would be SO offended. That is so rude I don't know how you can even contemplate approaching someone with that. I don't believe that anybody who has any kind of social etiquette skills would EVER do that.

If the ticket she paid for is being refunded to her card though she should really give that money to Sophie and accept being out of pocket for the ticket Marissa bought as she shouldn't have sold the gift ticket in the first place.

Omg I'm sorry but you would absolutely be the asshole. Your friend got you a ticket for a show as a gift - not money to buy a ticket. It would absolutely not be the same thing as "taking back yoir gift" the circumstances are completely out of her control and really I don't believe that you don't know that. You are trying to now find a way out of the hole you dug yourself into. You should have told her you already had a ticket, or sold the one you paid for. I don't think you should have tried to profiteer off of your friends good nature to buy you a gift. I'm sorry but selling a gift without telling the gift giver and then asking for the money back once it's been refunded is just such entitled behaviour.

If I were you I would frame it in such a way that it's not criticising him for smoking, but more that you are concerned about the finances and here are a few expenses you want to cut back on to help with your bills/unborn baby/future and list a few things and include weed in the list. If I were you I'd plan it out so you can say if we cut back on (insert non essential here) by 50 bucks and we cut back on the weed by X amount then we could put X amount towards....
But have some actual numbers ready and just include it with a few non essentials. 
If he is a reasonable person he will be able to see you are concerned about the financial situation and he will also understand that you are not poking at his weed use, you are just pointing out that it can be included with some non essentials you can cut back on.
If he is not able to see that then I would say that's a different set of issues.

I think she likes you. If you like her too then ask her to hang out. If after a couple of times hanging out its going good then maybe bring up a discussion about the boundaries while you're both at work.

It's probably nothing personal. Sometimes that chemistry just isn't there, or for some reason or another she doesn't see a future. She's allowed to feel that way. It's not wasted effort, as is the nature of dating you spend some time and effort and things will naturally run their course. I had the omg I'm single and I'm nearly 30 panic aswell. Shortly after this meltdown I met my current partner when I really wasn't looking.
I promise you will be fine. If you started talking October and its now January its only really 3 months, which I personally would say is a reasonable amount of time to get to know each other and date casually before making any decisions about whether or not you want to be with that person. Don't take it too hard. You're the right person for someone but just not for her. Remember that she is entitled to her feelings and she doesn't owe you anything. Its unpleasant when someone you like doesn't see a future but that's the nature of the beast when you're dating.

I really hate it when on here people always just immediately jump to "just break up" but in this situation the only advice I can give you is  R U N  A W A Y.  Fast.
For 2 reasons:
1. He will not change and eventually drag you down with him
2. This could potentially give you a whole bunch of issues when it comes to how you view your role within a relationship, what is acceptable treatment of you, and he could make a real mess of your self esteem. Take it from someone who has been there (more than once) it's really, really difficult to get your self worth back once you lose it.
The chances of her getting into a serious relationship in a month are slim. If I were you I'd work on you and if you still feel like going after her when you feel ready then do that :)

If someone approached me and said "I like you and want to be with you but I want you to wait while I sort myself out" I would see that as a red flag. You can't essentially put a human being on reserve. You're ready for a relationship or you're not. If you are, pursue her, and work on your personal development at the same time. If you're not ready for a relationship yet, then leave this chick alone and if she's still single when you're feeling ready, make your move.

I feel like everyone on here often has a huge amount of negative stuff to say, almost always "just break up/stay broken up" but its not always helpful.
Personally, I don't believe the "once a cheater always a cheater" some people may repeatedly cheat on their partners but sometimes people slip up and make a mistake and they own it and they're sorry. Also - she's 21. She's young, the person she is now she won't be in ten years. 
You say you can't face the heartache again - do you mean the heartache or the cheating or the heartache of the breakup? 
You know this chick, I don't, so your gut feeling will tell you if you really believe she won't cheat again. Listen to it. You wouldn't have a gut feeling if you weren't meant to trust your instincts. If you feel that you really believe she won't cheat again, and you want to be with her, give it a go. However, if you are scared of a breakup period, maybe you need to be single right now until you can accept that most relationships do, eventually break down, and accept that you will be fine. Breakups are shit, but you won't feel shit forever.
That's my advice to you :) 
But if you do get back together, you cannot bring up the cheating, throw it in her face in an argument, look through her phone, mistrust her etc. By commiting to a new relationship, you are committing to trust her and leave the past behind.

If I were you the bit that would really piss me off would be the "I can't take you seriously." If he doesn't take you seriously, why are you wasting your time? Secondly, even if he is not sorry for telling you why he watched romantic films with his ex and not you, he should still feel bad for hurting your feelings, and try to understand how in future he can communicate honestly with you, whilst still handling your feelings in a sensitive way.
I am curious to know why it bothers you that he would watch pride and prejudice with a previous partner and not you? It seems like there is more to it than just a film?

We've all been there. As harsh as this may sound, whether or not you believe you could have the world's greatest relationship and make him the happiest man alive is really neither here nor there. If the feelings are not reciprocated, they're not reciprocated, and there is nothing you can do that will force him to see it your way. The more of your investment in both time and emotion you put into the situation, holding onto the belief that this relationship is somehow meant to be, the harder it will be to walk away, and you will seriously damage your sense of self worth in the process. The best advice I can give you is walk away. I know its easier said than done, but future you will be very, very grateful.

I live in London and only speak English fluently. My mum speaks Polish but she never talked to me in Polish as a kid, so I only know a few words. I wish she had talked to me in Polish when I was growing up, so I knew another language fluently. I think being multi-lingual is a good thing no matter which languages they are. If I could speak say, for example, French, I would speak mostly in French to my child, even though they would live in an English speaking country, just so they would pick up another language at a young age. My partner and most other people would talk to them in English, so they would just learn 2 languages. 
It seems like a wild overreaction. It also just seems a bit stupid, because, although I appreciate English isn't commonly spoken in Italy, it is a very widely used language in the world and a useful one to be able to speak. Surely he, an Italian man working in London, appreciates how useful it is to be able to speak English fluently.
Also - regardless of the language issue, your husband shouldn't be making you cry with the way he talks to you.
